title: Protect the fair go in digital age, says ACTU
full_text:
ACTU secretary Melissa Donnelly has pressed the Senate inquiry into artificial intelligence to urge the Albanese government to implement regulatory protections for workers, backed by a regulator with enforcement powers, to ensure the “fair go is protected in the digital age”.
Ms Donnelly told the inquiry on Thursday that properly enforced regulatory protections must be a precondition of large US AI companies being able to train their models in Australia.
Unions are pressing for enhanced workers’ rights fit for the AI-age and national investment in sovereign AI capability to reduce reliance on US tech giants and to keep jobs and economic benefits flowing to Australians. Ms Donnelly said workers had almost no control over how AI was developed or used, have had their work stolen, and were experiencing job losses, intrusive monitoring and surveillance.
“It is the fundamental responsibility of this inquiry and our political leaders to ensure the fair go is protected in the digital age and that workers are safe, rights and conditions are protected and we have meaningful careers that we can build, especially for those young workers joining the workforce,” she said.
She said too many employers treated workers as robots and were introducing AI without basic transparency, meaningful consultation with workers, and in ways that were “degrading and intensifying work, making it more dangerous”.
She cited the decision this week by the National Australia Bank to cut 2500 jobs, saying the bank’s management initially refused to confirm to the Finance Sector Union if the cuts were associated with AI.
“This is a perfect example of the lack of transparency around these decisions that working people have experienced in workplace after workplace, in industry after industry,” she said.
“Despite NAB and other banks saying we need to grow and develop tech skills in Australia, they are slashing tech and engineering jobs. Now in damage control mode, NAB CEO Andrew Irvine went to the media to deny a connection with AI. If this is the case, why didn’t he communicate with his workers about this?” Ms Donnelly said the recent Medicare breach was a “watershed moment”, not only because it showed the capability of the technologies and how dangerous they could be, but because it showed the irresponsibility of the large, rich companies developing them.
“OpenAI keeps telling us what we must do to make it easier for them to develop their products here. We know they have knocked down doors to lobby for their changes when it suited them,” she said. “But when the risk was to us, to Australians, they couldn’t even be bothered to send an email to the right address. “The tech bros want us to believe that we as a country are powerless. But we are not; we absolutely can be an AI maker and not a taker. But we must do this based on our values, our social contract. This means protecting the fair go so we can pass it on to the next generation.“
